name: Squatmaxxing / spinal loading

lead: Squatmaxxing means training squats to build the quadriceps, glutes and lower body for more balanced, athletic proportions. Some users also ask whether it changes how tall or sturdy they look, and a looksmax.org thread discusses whether it suits people with a wide waist.

The squat is a compound exercise working the quadriceps, glutes, adductors and calves, with the spinal muscles and abdominals stabilising the trunk. Leg muscle growth from squatting is well established. The sources reviewed do not describe any effect on height, and spinal loading appears in height literature mainly through normal daily height variation.

paras: People add progressive squat training to a regular lifting routine, usually with leanness work so the legs and waist proportions show, and track changes in physique photos over months.
Wikipedia notes that poor form, especially over-flexing the torso, raises lower-back forces and can risk disc herniation. Heavy loading also compresses the spine temporarily.

angle.text: Heavy squat training builds the legs and glutes, giving more balanced, athletic proportions through added muscle. Leg growth from squatting is well established; no source ties squatting to a gain in height.

lead: Squatmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for building the legs and lower body through squats, either to improve physique proportions or, in some discussions, to affect how tall or strong a person looks. A looksmax.org thread titled Squatmaxxing asks whether leg development suits people with a wide waist, and a reply asks the original poster about body fat percentage, gym training and height.[1]

The sources reviewed describe the squat as a compound exercise working the quadriceps, glutes, adductors and calves, with the spinal erectors and abdominals acting as stabilisers.[2] They do not describe any effect of squatting on height.[2] The related idea of spinal loading, meaning compression of the spine under weight, is addressed in height literature mainly through daily height variation.[3]

paras: Wikipedia describes the squat as a lower-body exercise with many variants, including hack, Zercher and Steinborn squats named after early strength athletes.[2] The spine is loaded during barbell squats, and Wikipedia warns that over-flexing the torso greatly increases forces on the lower back and may risk disc herniation, while noting that padding and bracing are used to reduce spinal contact.[2]

Wikipedia reports that measured height varies over the day and that exercise just before measurement can lower the reading.[3] The squat article does not discuss height or spinal shrinkage.[2] No source reviewed claims that squatting changes adult stature.

Wikipedia cites a 2013 review by Hartmann and colleagues which concluded that deep squats performed with proper technique did not increase degenerative knee injury rates, and suggested shallower squats may be associated with long-term degeneration of the lumbar spine and knees.[2] The article itself carries a maintenance tag on source reliability.[2]
No studies found on squatting as a means of affecting height or appearance proportions in the sense used by looksmaxxing communities.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, squatmaxxing appears in a thread on whether leg training is useful for people described as wide-waisted.[1]

claims.claim: Squatting and leg development help people who are wide-waisted.
